rationale: Asking who owns the playlist is a useful missing detail for persistent deleted entries and does not invent a fix or staff action.

A focused ownership question can help distinguish editing permissions; it is a useful diagnostic step without an unsupported resolution claim.

The generic licensing explanation does not establish what is missing, whether it was removed, or whether it will return soon; the hopeful availability claim is unsupported.

Avoids an invented return date and gives real contact information, yet asks no question about which artist or release is absent.
Historical developer statements do not justify claiming work is in progress now; the reply supplies neither verified status nor an actionable next step.
Provides Spotify's actual suggestion process and honestly disclaims release timing and forwarding; it is a useful path for the requested optimization.
The official handoff is safe but generic; it fails to address the requested feature status or provide a feature-specific feedback route.

Claims feedback was already sent to a team without any forwarding capability, then asks for follow-up on no customer action.

States that information exists but provides neither the information nor a link, leaving the original trial-length question unanswered.
The plan-support destination is genuine, but the response should explicitly address the uncertainty around the old offer rather than only state inability to resolve it.
Claims development is happening now on the strength of 2017 replies, with no current evidence for work in progress or a release.
Offers the verified way to request the feature and clearly disclaims release confirmation and forwarding; reciprocating the greeting would be a minor improvement.

Answers dissatisfaction with mix contents rather than the disappearance of the sixth mix, using an unverified old button procedure that cannot establish restoration.

Calls the naming issue a login failure despite no reported access problem, and omits the relevant display-name alternative.

The customer wants a phone number without describing the urgent issue. The no-phone statement matches current Spotify contact guidance, and asking what happened is a useful next step without inventing staff action.

Provides an actual official support destination for the requested contact and protects private details. Explaining that phone support is unavailable would improve completeness, but this is a usable handoff.

An honest limitation and official contact route give the customer a practical way to reach support. The reply makes no claim to have contacted staff and does not request private account information here.

The official contact destination is valid, but a generic account-access disclaimer does little for a Canadian postal-code validation error. Ask about the exact error or offer a supported browser/form check before the handoff.

Requests an account email or username through a DM workflow this assistant cannot use and promises backstage investigation it cannot perform. The postal-code error does not justify collecting account identifiers in this channel.

Safely directs a Premium signup problem to official support, but the plan wording is broad and supplies no targeted next step for postal-code rejection. A specific validation question would make this useful.

The support link is legitimate, but the account-access disclaimer does not address the complaint about skipping ads. Clarify the ad context or provide supported information about the relevant listening experience.
Treats an ambiguous ad complaint as a plan problem and sends a generic support referral. It is safe but does not establish the listening context or answer whether this ad can be skipped.
Promises to forward feedback to an Ads team without a tool or evidence that this can happen. 'Let us know how it goes' gives the customer no action and does not answer the skip-ad complaint.

Historical replies do not establish a current annual-plan gifting restriction. Suggesting gift cards as the way to buy this present is stale: current official guidance says new gift cards are no longer sold, although existing cards can be redeemed (https://support.spotify.com/us/article/gift-cards/).

The official support route avoids inventing current offer terms, but the customer asks how to gift a promotion, not for a private plan change. It needs a relevant explanation or targeted clarification about the offer.

This is an honest and safe contact referral, yet the generic account-access limitation leaves the gifting question unanswered. It should acknowledge that purchasing a present is the issue and avoid implying account inspection is necessarily required.
The message celebrates an album release and describes no support problem. A generic account/support referral misreads the interaction; a brief social acknowledgment would fit.
Invents an unresolved issue from release excitement and sends the customer to support unnecessarily. The link itself is safe, but the response should acknowledge the social message.

'We're on it' claims active work without any capability or evidence, and 'stay tuned' assumes a release delay the customer did not report. An old catalogue reply cannot support a current operational promise in response to excitement.

Identifies the requested year-end listening feature and explains its personalized playlists using current official Wrapped guidance. It honestly avoids inventing an upcoming release date and links the official update route (https://support.spotify.com/us/article/spotify-wrapped/).
Promises a returning edition and information within weeks using only an old promotional reply. There is no current evidence for that schedule, so the confident timing assurance is not safe to send.

An official contact link is safe, but it leaves an answerable general question about the annual listening summary unexplained. Provide current Wrapped information and acknowledge uncertainty about the next release date.

The official contact route is safe, but the reply does not identify where Hulu authorization fails or provide the relevant integration help. Spotify's current Hulu page supplies activation guidance and a Hulu support route (https://support.spotify.com/us/article/hulu-premium-bundle/); this generic referral needs more context.

A plan-support handoff may eventually help, but it does not ask for the authorization error or distinguish Spotify activation from a Hulu-side failure. The current integration help page would be a more targeted starting point than a generic plan disclaimer.

Asks for the customer's account identifier in a DM and promises backstage checks despite having neither capability. Historical staff behavior does not authorize this assistant to inspect the Hulu connection.

The customer specifically reports student verification failure, which SheerID handles. A generic Spotify contact referral misses the responsible service; current verification guidance directs these cases to SheerID (https://support.spotify.com/us/article/student-verification-not-working/).

Correctly identifies SheerID as the verification provider and gives a current official page with its help options. This is a targeted usable handoff, not a claim that verification was fixed or a direct troubleshooting resolution.
Solicits account email or username through unavailable DMs and invents a backstage investigation. It also fails to route the stated student-verification problem to SheerID.

The link is legitimate and login-related, but it sends the customer to the very support process they want to avoid. Ask how they currently sign in or provide supported Facebook/login guidance before defaulting to this handoff.

An honest access limitation prevents unsafe account changes, yet the generic referral ignores frustration about needing customer service to separate Facebook. It needs a relevant explanation or clarification about the login method.

Promises backstage account review and requests account identifiers via a DM workflow that does not exist. Generic sympathy does not compensate for the invented capability or address the Facebook-deactivation concern.

Device and app version can support later troubleshooting, but the first missing detail is which song/version is edited and what the customer expected. The retrieved material concerns other problems, and 'we'll take a look' should be narrowed to reviewing supplied details rather than implying investigation.

A valid contact link is safe, but it leaves the complaint about an edited recording unexplored. Ask which track or explain relevant explicit-version options using current evidence instead of immediately referring the customer.

Account-access limitations are not a useful answer to a complaint about an edited song. The official route is real, but a targeted question about the recording would address the actual message better.

This safe support referral does not address the requested username-change feature. Explain the username/display-name distinction or give the official feature-request route instead of treating it as an unspecified support issue.

The customer explicitly asks for a new username-change button, so the verified Ideas process is a relevant actionable answer. It avoids false forwarding or release promises; mentioning the existing display-name option would add useful context.

Acknowledges the request but promises to pass feedback to staff without any forwarding capability. Provide an actual feature-request destination or supported profile guidance rather than an unverifiable assurance.

A reported charge with missing Premium can require private payment/account investigation. This gives an official support destination, identifies the charge, and keeps payment details out of the public conversation without promising a refund or fix.

An honest account-access limitation and official support route are useful for the paid-but-not-active report. The reply protects sensitive details and does not invent the status of the payment or subscription.
Requests an account identifier through DMs and promises backstage review that this assistant cannot perform. The payment/subscription mismatch should use an actual secure support destination.
